titleText.es: La única diferencia importante que he visto está en los colores. Cuando el texto normal dice "pulsar el botón rojo", el texto en braille dice "pulsar el botón de dos centímetros".
titleText.en: The only big difference I've seen is in colors. Where the regular text reads “press red button,” the braille reads “press two-inch button.”
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive localizes the original two-inch measurement as two centimeters.

regions.labelEs: HACE UN TIEMPO QUE APRENDÍ A LEER BRAILLE, Y ME HE DADO CUENTA DE QUE LOS MENSAJES DE LOS CARTELES NO SIEMPRE CONCUERDAN CON EL TEXTO NORMAL.

applications.explanationEn: Hace comes before un tiempo to place the following event a while in the past.
Here que connects the elapsed-time phrase to the event it dates; natural English usually restructures the wording rather than translating que alone.
Aprendí changes for the speaker and past time, while a introduces leer in its unchanged dictionary form.
He marks a completed action connected to the present, and dado is dar's completed-action form.

applications.exampleEs: ME HE DADO CUENTA DE QUE
applications.explanationEn: Me matches the speaker; he dado supplies the completed form of dar; cuenta completes the fixed expression; and de que introduces the fact noticed.
Concuerdan is the plural form because the things being compared are plural, and con introduces what they are matched against.

excludedUnits.rationale: These visible Braille cells encode an English message rather than printed Spanish lexical material.

applications.explanationEn: Tercera comes before planta and uses the feminine -a ending to match that feminine singular noun.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

example.es: Llegué hace dos horas.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.

example.es: Nos conocimos hace tres meses.

cards.answerEn: since; no separate English word in a natural ‘a while ago’ translation
cards.noteEn: After hace and an amount of elapsed time, que can connect that time to the event being dated. English often restructures the idea rather than translating que by itself.

example.es: Hace un mes que hablé con Ana.
example.en: I spoke with Ana a month ago.

cards.promptEs: aprender a + verbo en su forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone learns how to do an activity?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of aprender, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only aprender changes for the person and time. The action after a stays in its dictionary form—the form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. English normally uses ‘learn to’ before the action.

example.es: Marta aprende a nadar.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)
Braille and printed lettering can encode different messages on the same sign.
cards.noteEn: The joke relies on many sighted readers being unable to check the raised-dot text. A sign can therefore look ordinary in print while its Braille carries a private, hostile message.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.es: Me quejo del ruido.

cards.promptEs: darse cuenta de (que) + hecho o situación
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone realizes or becomes aware of something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun, a form of dar, cuenta, and then de before what is realized.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun and dar must match the person: me doy cuenta, te das cuenta, se da cuenta, nos damos cuenta, and so on. Use de before a noun and de que before a full statement. Cuenta is not translated separately in this expression.

example.es: Nos dimos cuenta de que faltaba una llave.
example.en: We realized that a key was missing.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.es: He terminado.

cards.answerEn: realized; noticed (as part of me he dado cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Dado is the completed-action form of dar, normally ‘given.’ Inside darse cuenta, the whole expression means ‘to realize’ or ‘to notice,’ so dado is not translated as ‘given.’

example.es: Me he dado cuenta del error.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes darse cuenta, “to realize”
cards.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account, bill, or calculation. In darse cuenta, it is part of a fixed expression and is not translated separately.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta muy tarde.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces what is realized after darse cuenta
cards.noteEn: After darse cuenta, de introduces the fact or thing that becomes clear. Before a full statement, Spanish normally uses de que.

example.es: Se dio cuenta de que era tarde.
example.en: She realized that it was late.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.es: Creo que Ana viene.
example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: on; belonging to (linking content to a sign or notice)
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use de to connect a message or wording to the sign that contains it. Natural English often says that the message is ‘on’ the sign.

example.es: El mensaje del cartel es muy claro.
example.en: The message on the sign is very clear.

cards.promptEs: concordar con + persona, idea o cosa
cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing agrees with or matches another?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of concordar followed by con and the person, idea, or thing it matches.
cards.noteEn: Concordar changes for who or what agrees. Con introduces the other side of the match. Depending on context, English can use ‘agree with,’ ‘match,’ or ‘be consistent with.’

example.es: Los datos concuerdan con el informe.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; links concordar to what matches
cards.noteEn: Concordar uses con before the person, statement, or thing that agrees or matches. English may translate concordar con simply as ‘to match.’

example.es: La copia no concuerda con el original.
example.en: The copy does not match the original.

cards.noteEn: Tercera is the feminine form of tercero, ‘third.’ Its ending matches a feminine singular noun such as planta or puerta.

example.es: Es la tercera puerta.

cards.promptEs: número ordinal antes de un sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you use words such as first, second, or third before a Spanish noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the ordinal before the noun and make its ending match the noun's gender and number.
cards.noteEn: An ordinal gives a position in an order. Primero, segundo, tercero, último, and similar words usually come before the noun. Most forms use -o with a masculine singular noun and -a with a feminine singular noun, but primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun. Plural nouns use plural forms.

example.es: La segunda puerta está en el tercer piso.
example.en: The second door is on the third floor.

cards.noteEn: Planta can mean a plant, the sole of a foot, or a floor in a building. On an elevator sign or building directory, planta means a floor of a building.

example.es: La oficina está en la tercera planta.
example.en: The office is on the third floor.

cards.answerEn: the (masculine plural; the letters spell los)
cards.noteEn: Hyphens between individual letters show a word being read out one letter at a time. Read l-o-s together as los.

example.es: C-A-S-A forma la palabra casa.

cards.answerEn: sighted people; people who can see (spelled out)
cards.noteEn: Read the separated letters together as videntes. Vidente can also mean a seer or clairvoyant, but here it contrasts people who can see with people who read Braille by touch.

example.es: La señal tiene texto para personas videntes.
example.en: The sign has text for sighted people.

cards.answerEn: they suck; they are awful (spelled out, informal)
cards.noteEn: Read the separated letters together as apestan. The literal meaning is ‘they stink’; informally, the same verb can say that people or things are terrible.

example.es: Esas reglas apestan.

cards.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.es: Oye, necesito hablar contigo.
example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.
